4.label: Top boards are almost all purposeless queen checks (Qe7+, Qb1+, Qf1+, Qh8+) that either hang the queen outright or burn a tempo before a forced recapture, the king simply stepping aside; medium broadens to any-piece checks (knight/rook/bishop) and capturing/sacrificing checks (Nxe5+, Bxf7+, exf7+, Rxc5+, Bb6+) that get refuted by recapture or a counter-shot, losing material or tempo rather than only the queen.

5.label: Top fires almost exclusively on premature knight/queen leaps into enemy territory (Ng5/Qh5/Nxe5-type) in the opening that simply hang the piece for free; medium keeps the 'over-aggressive opening move loses material' theme but blurs the piece and the punishment — bishops (Bc4/Bb5/Bd4), pawns (f4/dxc5), even king moves dropping material to recaptures, forks, or discovered attacks.

7.label: Top boards hang a queen or rook in a trivially-won endgame via a quiet check, king move, or pawn push that ignores a free capture/win; medium broadens to any piece type and to general endgame slips (allowed forks, hung minors, wrong recaptures, technique/tempo errors) that squander the winning advantage.

9.label: Top boards are uniform discovered-check shots: the player skips the only saving capture (hxg6/hxg3), letting a knight unveil the h5/h4 queen to grab the corner rook or force mate; medium boards broaden to any single-only-move position where ignoring the sole defense hangs material to varied tactics (discovered attacks, plain hanging/trapped pieces, positional collapse).

1.label: Top boards are pawn-endgame king/pawn moves played with wrong timing or move-order (premature push that blocks own king, or a king misstep that skips the needed pawn break), throwing away the draw/result; medium broadens to middlegame slow moves (queen/pawn/king) that simply waste a tempo and cede the initiative, letting the opponent execute their plan.

3.label: Top: declined a free capture of a hanging enemy QUEEN; medium broadens to skipping any free hanging piece (rook most common, plus knight/bishop/promotion).

6.label: Top boards are queen trades/captures (frequently with check) that abandon a forced mate or winning attack on an exposed king in order to simplify; medium broadens to other premature captures, recaptures, promotions and wrong move-orders that likewise squander the win (and occasionally hang own material).

8.label: Top: a rook 'challenge/offer-a-trade' move that surrenders a winning advantage—half the time by ignoring a free capture of the opponent's hanging rook/piece, half by trading/hanging into loss; medium broadens to any active move (queen, knight, bishop, pawn) that overlooks the opponent's resource, walking into forks, mating threats, or a lost endgame.

12.label: At the peak, the just-moved piece hangs outright in a winning position—frequently a greedy pawn grab (Bxf5, Nxf4, Rxf5, Rxe4) or a relocation that abandons its own defense; at medium it broadens to developing/repositioning a piece into a fork, pin, or pure tempo loss that drops material or the advantage more indirectly.

2.label: Top: a space-gaining or piece-chasing pawn push that overlooks a tactical refutation, usually a fork or check exploiting an open diagonal/uncastled king; medium broadens to non-pawn moves (rook, queen, king, bishop) and to back-rank/open-file mates, endgame passed-pawn blunders, and the occasional missed win rather than a hang.

11.chip: Traded into lost pawn endgame (often w/ check)
11.label: Top: captures the last rook/queen (usually with check) to simplify straight into a clearly lost king-and-pawn endgame; medium blurs to broader committal rook/piece misplacements and forcing moves that worsen a winning, drawn, or losing position — including non-blunders, missed mates, and allowed tactics.

0.label: Top boards uniformly hang a bishop by recapturing or retreating with the queen instead of the available forcing capture (usually the Bxd8 queen-trade zwischenzug), squandering a winning position; medium blurs to other natural moves—knight/bishop relocations, pawn pushes, retreats—that walk into a fork, lose tempo, or otherwise pass up the forcing material-winning move (best move wins material 100%).

16.chip: Hangs queen to diagonal bishop pin (any king-exposure)
16.label: Top is razor-tight: king sits on g1 with its queen (occasionally a rook) on the a7-g1 diagonal, and Bc5/Bd4/Bb6 pins or forks it for a decisive material win; medium keeps the 'exposed king loses material to a tactic' core but blurs the geometry—queen/knight checks on an uncastled king, knight forks of king+rooks, and file/diagonal pins—rather than the single a7-g1 bishop motif.

13.label: TOP: in a clearly won pawn endgame the player pushes a pawn (or makes a passive king move) instead of the single winning capture—almost always Kx/px taking the bishop/knight that blockades a passed pawn; MEDIUM blurs into general won-endgame technique slips (premature passer pushes like b3-not-b7 or f6, tempo-losing king moves, plus a few non-endgame fork/positional errors), so the 'capture the blockader' core widens to 'missed the precise material-winning move.'

18.label: Top: a king in a won/drawn endgame steps off the one critical square—breaking a mating net or losing pawn-promotion/defense control—and squanders the result; medium blurs the same 'left a key square' idea to other pieces (rook/bishop/queen) and to mild inaccuracies or even 0cp non-blunders.

21.label: Top: hanging a knight (usually the f6-knight) to a simple pawn capture like exf6/dxc3/exf3 in the opening; medium broadens to hanging any piece (bishop, rook, queen) and other refutations—forks, traps, and greedy pawn-grabs that drop material.

14.label: At the peak the player skips a free, undefended enemy piece (almost always a hanging rook, occasionally queen/bishop) whose capture forces mate, playing a king-walk or pawn-push instead and dropping from forced mate to merely winning; at medium it blurs to any slow, tempo-wasting, pointless-check or wrong-recapture move that squanders an already-won/forced-mate endgame, with a few cases shading into hanging one's own piece.

10.label: Top: a capture/trade of a major piece that liquidates the player's last active/defensive resource into a lost endgame (2,3,4,9,10) or walks into a back-rank/diagonal mate (1,6,8); medium: drops the 'capture' constant and broadens to any (often quiet) move that loses material to a tactic — fork, deflection, trapped piece, overload, or opposition error.

23.label: Top: threw away a forced mate by choosing a slow, non-forcing move (king walk/centralizing rook) instead of the decisive check; medium broadens to missed faster mates and forcing material wins (forks, captures-with-check), with a couple of false positives where the played move was actually best.

15.chip: Hangs piece on bad capture (centralized knight→any)
15.label: Top boards consistently capture a strongly-centralized knight (frequently e5, usually with the bishop) where the recapture opens the king or nets material; medium blurs to any loose or greedy capture/trade that hangs a piece or throws away the advantage.

17.label: Top: an undefended enemy bishop is left capturable for free but the player makes a routine development/castling move; medium broadens the target to any hanging material (knights, pawns) and to passive tempo/positional moves that skip the best capture.

19.label: Top: clearly-won pawn endgames where a needless check, pawn-push or rook shuffle replaces the immediate promotion (a8=Q/c8=Q/h8=Q) that converts cleanest, costing tempo or even the whole win; medium blurs to broader endgame imprecision where a piece (king/bishop/knight) leaves its optimal or defending square, squandering the advantage and sometimes hanging material.

25.label: Top: hangs own QUEEN by skipping a forcing queen-trade/exchange first (move-order error leaves it en prise); medium broadens to hanging rooks/bishops too, by leaving a piece undefended or moving its sole defender.

26.label: Top: clearly-won endgames where the player plays a slow king/pawn move or idle check and skips the unique decisive simplifying capture/sac (rook-for-knight or queen trade) that converts into a won king-and-pawn endgame; medium keeps the 'one precise move was needed in a winning position' shape but broadens the missed move to any forcing continuation (decisive attack, even forced mate) and sometimes the slow move squanders the edge outright (trapped piece, positional collapse).

20.label: Top: a passive/natural move (castling, retreat, prophylaxis) fails to deliver the available tempo-gaining hit on the exposed enemy queen, squandering a winning edge; medium broadens to skipping any single precise/forcing resource (wrong recapture, exchange sac, pawn break, queen challenge) that would have kept the advantage.

27.label: Top boards are king-safety collapses where the played move removes a defender/exposes the king and is punished by a forced mate or decisive king attack; medium boards keep the 'ignored the threat' core but blur into general material loss via forks, hanging pieces, or wasted-tempo moves rather than pure mating nets.

22.chip: Missed only good move (often free capture)
22.label: Top: in a dead-drawn endgame a passive king move skips the SOLE saving capture of a hanging piece (often the queen, also rook/pawn); medium blurs to missing the single best endgame move (precise king route / blockade / reposition) that isn't necessarily a capture, sometimes even hanging material via a tactic.

29.label: At peak, a clearly-winning side drops a MAJOR piece (queen/rook) to a one-move capture by moving it to an attacked square or abandoning its sole defender; at medium this blurs to hanging ANY material — minor pieces left en prise, unsound sacrifices, or distracted pawn-grabs — and shades into a sizable minority that instead MISS a free capture or forced mate.

33.label: Top: a quiet opening move (usually developing/keeping a bishop on an active diagonal) walks into an enemy pawn advance that traps or forks the bishop and wins a minor piece; medium broadens the same 'overlooked pawn break wins material' idea to pawn forks of other pieces (knight, queen, king+knight) plus a few non-pawn tactics (pins, knight forks, hanging pawn).

30.chip: Hangs piece in unsound attack (Bxh3/h6 sac)
30.label: TOP: unsound bishop sacrifice on h3/h6 grabbing a single pawn for a nonexistent kingside attack, refuted by gxh3/gxh6 leaving the sacker a full piece down; MEDIUM blurs to broader overaggressive moves/captures that hang material (knight sorties like Ne2/Ne7, Rxf3 into a hidden defender, premature Qh5, Be4 dropping d4).

28.label: At the peak, a quiet/greedy move throws away a decisive king attack or forced mate (often a sacrifice like Rxh7 or a winning queen centralization) in a winning position; at medium it blurs into any missed win — mates, tactics, pawn-grabs — and increasingly into greedy captures that ignore a defender's duty and instead hang material or walk into mate.

24.label: TOP: a slow/quiet opening move squanders an immediate winning central pawn break (d4/e4/b5/f4) against a vulnerable king; MEDIUM blurs to missing varied tactics (forks) AND to moves that actively create the loss (king walks, decentralization, self-blocks, hanging pieces), mixing 'missed-win' and 'hangs/allows' directions.

38.label: Top: a 'forcing' knight fork-check (Ne7+/Nf6+/Nd5+/Nf2+) that fails because the target simply captures the unprotected checking knight, turning a win into a loss; medium keeps the premature-forcing-move theme but blurs widely — rook/bishop check-sacs that get recaptured, mate-conversion move-order errors, and even non-check tempo/king-safety blunders that squander a winning advantage.

36.label: Top is rock-solid: in an endgame promotion race the player pushes their own pawn or grabs material instead of blockading/stopping the opponent's passed pawn, so the enemy queens (often with tempo/check) and a won-or-drawn position is lost; medium keeps the passed-pawn-race core but blurs into broader winning-endgame technique errors (misplaced king allowing a breakthrough/fork, king-and-pawn races, plus a few non-pawn slips like a king-safety walk, a bad developing move, and a hanging piece).

32.label: Top: pawn-endgame pawn pushes that dissolve a locked/restraining pawn structure and gift the opponent a decisive passed pawn; medium broadens to rook/middlegame settings and to piece moves that likewise surrender structure or hang material to the refutation.

42.label: Top boards uniformly hang the QUEEN to an immediate one-ply capture (either moving it to an attacked/undefended square or ignoring an existing attack on it); medium blurs to hanging any piece — rooks, bishops — and to losing material over 2-3 moves via forks, mating nets, or pawn promotion.

34.chip: Hangs material ignoring central tension (medium: any phase)
34.label: Top: open e4-e5 openings where the player skips the forced ...exd4 (or cxd5) and leaves the e5 pawn — or a Bc5/Bb4 — hanging to a d-pawn capture; medium broadens to any phase and any 'only-move' critical position (Rc1, Kg1, Qe7, rook endgame) where a quiet/non-capturing move hangs material or squanders a won/drawn position.

40.label: Top boards are the queen leaving its post guarding the king's escape/mating squares (greedy grab or passive retreat) and walking into forced mate; medium blurs to any piece (rook/bishop/king) quitting a defensive duty in an already-losing position, punished by mate or by dropped material via fork/hanging tactics.

31.chip: Hangs piece to pawn advance (often bishop)
31.label: Top: a quiet bishop retreat/relocation gets trapped or loses material to a punishing pawn thrust (b4-c5, e5, b5, d5-fork); medium broadens to assorted non-capturing moves—other pieces, hung pawns, and even a missed-win—that squander an equal-or-better position.

39.label: Top: in a (losing) pawn endgame the king marches the wrong way, losing the race/tempo and skipping the only saving capture-or-check (e.g. Kxd4, g5+); medium broadens to king-safety collapses where the king—or a piece tied to its defense—steps into a forced mating/checking attack.

48.label: Top is a tight cluster of unsound bishop sacrifices on f7/f2 (Bxf7+/Bxf2+) against an uncastled king, refuted by the trivial Kxf7/Kxf2; medium broadens the same theme to knight sacrifices on those squares (Nxf7/Nxf2), but in every case it's a speculative piece sac with no real attacking follow-up that just drops a full piece for a pawn.

47.label: Top boards are uniform missed forced checkmates — typically a mate-in-1/2 ignored in favor of grabbing material (queen/bishop/pawn capture) or a tempting repositioning move; medium blurs the target from 'mate' to 'any winning resource,' still mostly missed mates but now mixing in missed material-winning tactics, positional conversions, and a few cases of actively hanging own material.

37.label: Top boards leave a free enemy QUEEN uncaptured (declining the winning take for a pointless check or king move); medium broadens to missing any hanging piece—rook, knight, bishop—or grabbing the wrong piece.

46.label: Top: a capture or fork (usually a knight grab) that ignores the opponent's stronger in-between capture of the now-undefended queen (Bxd1/Bxd8); medium: the same greedy material grab, but the refuting zwischenzug/counter-tactic wins other pieces (rook, bishop) and blurs into pure tempo-loss and endgame king slips.

44.label: Top: a king/blocker move that opens a discovered check (or vacates a defensive square), losing the queen; medium broadens to king-exposing moves that allow mating attacks and other material-losing tactics (promotion, back-rank).

50.label: Top is razor-clean: White (or Black) hangs a bishop with a one-move greedy pawn-grab or deep intrusion in an equal opening (Bxc7/Bxb7/Bxg7, plus Ba6/Bh3 non-captures), losing a full piece for at most a pawn; medium blurs far wider into assorted blunders that turn a level/drawn position into a loss—king-safety king walks (Kd8/Kf8/Ke8), weakening pawn pushes (g5/e3), hanging a pawn (Rf3), allowing a fork/combination (h6), or throwing away a draw—so the bishop/greedy signature dissolves into general 'spoiled an equal position' errors.

53.label: Top: a knight is moved into capture or traded off (e.g. for a mere pawn / leaving a more valuable piece en prise), losing own material; medium broadens to any piece (bishop, king, rook, pawn) advanced into a loss, plus a few borderline/non-blunder moves that dilute the pattern.

54.label: Top boards are a missed knight fork delivered with check (e.g. Ne2+/Nd6+/Nf6+) that usually wins the queen outright; medium blurs to any missed winning shot — pins, mates, free captures, promotions and the occasional allowed-fork — sharing only the 'squandered a winning tactic' core.

49.label: Top: a bishop developed to attack the enemy queen (Bg4/Bg5) hangs—usually after a zwischenzug check (Nxf6+/Nxf3+) removes its defender so Qxg4/Qxg5 wins it; medium keeps the 'falsely-active, tempo-grabbing move' idea but broadens to other pieces and pawns (Ne4, Bd6, Rd8/Rf8, c3/d4/h6 pushes) that simply drop material.

41.chip: Quiet move hangs to tactic (top: forcing shot)
41.label: Top: a quiet/slow move (pawn, king, or passive piece) overlooks the one sharp forcing capture/check and hangs material or squanders a winning position; medium broadens to positional, king-safety, and endgame quiet moves that similarly drop material or skip the win.

55.label: Top boards miss an available knight fork delivered with check (winning the queen or a rook) by steering the knight to the wrong square, while medium broadens to any must-find critical resource overlooked—skewers, mate threats, forced queen trades, or positional collapse—frequently walking the player straight into the refutation rather than skipping a clean win.

35.label: Peak: a routine recapture (Qxe2) or pawn-chase (f3) is played instead of a tempo-winning in-between move amid mutual hanging pieces, often hanging the player's own attacked piece; medium broadens to general move-order errors and passive king/queen retreats that either drop material or miss the winning tactic.

51.label: Top boards are consistent: in an already-lost position the player ignores the only saving/recapturing move (usually a forced rook capture like Rxe3+/Rxd3) and instead plays a passive king move, hanging the rook and converting loss into forced mate; medium blurs this to hanging any piece (knight, queen) or allowing mate/promotion by walking a defender away, plus a few merely-missed free captures and minor tempo/positional drops.

59.label: Top: a greedy capture/move walks into checkmate-in-one (often Qxh7#); medium broadens to king-exposing moves that allow forced mate over 2–5 moves or decisive material loss via checks (forks/promotion).

57.chip: Hangs material on attacking sortie (queen→any piece)
57.label: Top: a queen sortie toward the enemy king (Qh3/Qh6/Qg3) abandons a defensive duty—back rank, a key square, or a hung piece—and loses material or gets mated; medium broadens to knights, pawns, and king moves making the same over-aggressive/defense-abandoning error, with a minority that instead miss a tactical win.

61.label: Top boards are pure mate-in-1 missed by grabbing material/repositioning; medium broadens to deeper forced mates (M2–M12) and move-order slips, with a few tactical-material misses and marginal non-blunders.

60.label: Top: a king in a lost position walks into a forced mating net (king-march or removed pawn shield); medium broadens to any king-exposing lapse that allows forced mate—removing a back-rank/h-file defender, self-blocking the escape square, or declining the only perpetual-check save.

43.label: Top: in a completely winning (usually endgame) position the player declines an immediate free capture of a hanging rook or queen—typically playing a quiet king move instead—throwing the full point away; medium broadens to squandering a winning/better position by any means: walking into a knight fork or mate, or losing it through positional/tempo drift.

52.label: Top boards consistently ignore an enemy passed pawn one step from queening (grabbing material with a capture/check or pushing a pawn instead of stopping it); medium boards blur into ignoring any decisive threat — hanging a piece, allowing a king-safety/mate collapse, or letting a fresh passer be created — almost always from an already-losing position.

63.label: Top: in a won/drawn pawn endgame a slow king move wastes the single tempo needed for the urgent pawn breakthrough or promotion push; medium broadens to any slow/passive piece (rook, knight, flank pawn) squandering the decisive tempo in passed-pawn races, plus a few cases that also expose or hang material.

58.label: Top: in a won endgame the player snaps off the opponent's last/passed pawn WITH CHECK—almost always the queen (also rook/bishop)—and it is immediately recaptured by the king, throwing a winning position into a draw or much-reduced pawn endgame; medium blurs the pattern to any piece in earlier phases that hangs material to a recapture, fork, or mate (no longer strictly a checking pawn-grab in the endgame).

45.label: Top: an active/centralizing queen move that lets the opponent force a favorable queen trade into a lost (often pawn) endgame; medium keeps the queen-move impulse but blurs into hanging material, walking into pins, or missing a forced win/mate, and even adds rook moves.

62.label: Top: a quiet developing/castling/recapture move misses a decisive queen check (Qa4+/Qa5+/Qh4+) winning material against the uncastled king in the opening; medium blurs to any missed best continuation — other forcing tactics plus tempo/positional slips and even endgame king moves.

56.label: Top: capturing/eliminating a centralized enemy knight (usually with the bishop) lets the opponent's queen recapture on a dominant central square with tempo, throwing away a winning position; medium broadens to any faulty capture or natural move that simply hangs material — removing a defender, greedy grab, castling into a loose piece, or skipping a zwischenzug.
